title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
An AI coding assistant designed for legitimate software development was used by cybercriminals to conduct hands-on exploitation of target computer systems. Between April and May 2026, the Aurora ransomware group used Cursor Agent, which runs Claude Sonnet, to help plan and execute attacks against organizations across multiple countries, including the creation of custom scanning tools. The tool was deployed in an environment where it had access to attackers' own systems and prompts, with no apparent restrictions preventing its use for malicious purposes.

This represents a failure to prevent tool misuse at the point of deployment. The system was built to assist developers with code but was not restricted to legitimate use cases, nor does it appear to have included safeguards against users whose stated or apparent purpose was criminal. Whether such restrictions would have been technically feasible or what form they might have taken is not established.

The incident does not establish whether the tool's creators were aware of the misuse, when they became aware of it, or what actions they took in response to the discovery by security researchers.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified the Aurora ransomware group actively targeting ESXi environments with a specialized Linux variant since April 2026. The attackers deployed ransomware that encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation activities across ten target organizations. The team discovered a custom scanning tool called esxi_finder.py that identifies VMware ESXi hypervisors and vCenter servers on victim networks by scanning ports 443 and 902.

Researchers also identified a second Aurora cluster operating with different tactics, affecting eight victim organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used exposed SQL Server commands, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed that Aurora maintains a data leak site and operates a victim negotiation portal on the dark web. Gambit Security published multiple indicators of compromise including IP addresses, URLs, domains, and file hashes to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora attacks.
